title: Pesto
subtitle: Genoese basil sauce with pine nuts, Parmesan, and garlic
excerpt: A vibrant green Genoese sauce made by pounding fresh basil with pine nuts, garlic, Parmesan, and good olive oil. Stir through pasta, spoon over soup, or use as a dressing.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pesto (from the Genoese pestare, to pound) is the defining sauce of Ligurian cuisine, made in its traditional form with a marble mortar and wooden pestle. The name is also the source of the English word pestle. The classic Genoese recipe specifies: Genovese basil DOP (Denominazione di Origine Protetta), Ligurian extra-virgin olive oil, Parmigiano-Reggiano, Pecorino Sardo (or Pecorino Romano), pine nuts, garlic, and sea salt. In the traditional method the ingredients are pounded progressively in the mortar, starting with the garlic and salt, then the pine nuts, then the basil, and finally the cheese and oil are worked in. The food processor version is faster but produces a slightly different (more emulsified, less textured) result. Pesto is a raw sauce: it should never be cooked, as heat turns the basil brown and kills the fresh flavour. It is stirred through hot pasta off the heat, with a little pasta cooking water to loosen, rather than added to the pan.

content.text: The key to a bright green pesto is to work quickly and not overheat the basil: the friction of a food processor can warm the sauce enough to darken it. Chill the food processor bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes before use, or blanch and refresh the basil briefly (3 seconds in boiling water, then immediately into iced water) to preserve its colour for a day. A pesto made with a mortar and pestle will always be slightly coarser and more vibrant than a blended version: both are excellent. Add the olive oil last and in a stream.

items.preparation: leaves only, packed; about 2 large bunches
finely grated; or use all Parmesan

content.text: Put the basil, garlic, pine nuts, and salt in a food processor. Pulse until finely chopped. Scrape down the sides. Add the Parmesan and Pecorino and pulse again.
With the motor running, pour in the olive oil in a thin stream. Stop as soon as combined: the pesto should have some texture. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

To serve with pasta: stir through freshly cooked, drained pasta off the heat, loosening with a few tablespoons of the pasta cooking water. The pesto should coat the pasta without clumping. Store in a jar with olive oil poured over the surface to prevent browning. Keeps for up to 5 days in the fridge.
